svg.title: Three routes to data centre micro-segmentation - fabric, host, and hybrid - and how to choose between them
svg.desc: Top: the traffic argument. Most east-west traffic never leaves the data centre, so if the security budget went into north-south egress firewalls while the inside of the data centre is one large VLAN, the real exposure sits exactly where nothing is watching. Middle: three routes. The network side enforces policy in the fabric with EPG and ACI or VXLAN security groups, which suits new data centres and private cloud but binds the design to one vendor architecture and carries a high migration cost. The host side enforces policy in the operating system kernel through an agent, eBPF or a container CNI, which suits virtualisation and container-heavy estates and hybrid cloud, but requires agents and covers neither bare metal nor network devices. The hybrid route - coarse segmentation at the east-west entry in the fabric, fine segmentation inside the host - is the most realistic answer and costs a mapping between two policy systems. Bottom: the three questions that decide it - is there bare metal or appliances that cannot run an agent; who owns the policy, the network team or the application team; and when one intent has two sources of truth, which system wins. A closing note says the hybrid route only works if the two policy systems have a documented precedence rule, otherwise incident response starts by guessing which layer blocked the flow.
svg.text: The data centre: most of the traffic never crosses the firewall you bought
East-west inside the fabric is the bulk of the volume, and it is also where lateral movement lives
WHERE THE VOLUME ACTUALLY GOES
east-west inside the data centre - server to server, pod to pod, VM to VM
north-south
internet
If the investment is all in the small green bar while the red bar is one large VLAN, the exposure is exactly where nothing is watching.
ROUTE 1 · NETWORK SIDE
EPG / ACI · VXLAN + security groups
Policy enforced in the fabric, in front of
the workload, independent of the OS
Fits: new data centres, private cloud,
a greenfield fabric decision
Cost: bound to one vendor architecture,
high migration cost, needs a fabric team
Contract question: what happens to policy
when we leave this architecture?
Answer it before signing, not after.
ROUTE 2 · HOST SIDE
agent · eBPF · container CNI
Policy enforced in the kernel, next to the
process, following the workload anywhere
Fits: virtualisation and container dense,
hybrid and multi-cloud estates
Cost: an agent on every host; covers
neither bare metal nor network devices
The uncovered bare-metal box is usually the
database that matters most - plan a
network-side island around it
ROUTE 3 · HYBRID
coarse in the fabric, fine in the host
East-west entry point segmented by the
network; inside the host the policy is fine
Fits: almost every real migration - it
lets the network and platform teams move
at their own pace
Cost: a mapping between two policy
systems, and a precedence rule nobody
wants to write
Write the precedence rule anyway.
THREE QUESTIONS THAT DECIDE WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ACTUALLY ON

g.text: Is there bare metal or an appliance that cannot run an agent? Then the network side must cover it.
Who owns the intent - the network team or the application team? Ownership follows the change process.
When both layers can block a flow, which one wins? Undocumented, this is the first hour of every incident.

svg.text: The hybrid route is not a compromise - it is the only route that admits the two teams deploy at different speeds. What it must not be is undocumented.
